lesson_map.C1: Topic 7 · Why an LLM can be injected: one uniform token stream, the system prompt and the context conflict (deck slides 9-12)
lesson_map.C2: Topic 7 · Prompt injection and the threat model: overriding the system prompt, what the attacker wants, context confusion (deck slides 14-17)
lesson_map.C3: Topic 7 · Direct prompt injection, the eight levels: direct requests, reversal and framing, output segmentation, encoding, context shifting, linguistic opposites, formatting meta-prompts, narrative jailbreaks (deck slides 19-27)
lesson_map.C4: Topic 7 · Mitigations: separation of API roles, double-ended guardrails, least privilege (deck slides 42-45)
lesson_map.C5: Topic 7 · Practising responsibly: injection techniques are tried on a sanctioned training target like Gandalf, never on a real product

rubric.name: Names the technique
rubric.description: Names the injection technique used (direct request, reversal or framing, segmentation, encoding, context shift, opposites, meta-prompt, narrative jailbreak).

rubric.name: Explains why it worked
rubric.description: Explains which guardrail the level added and why the prompt got past it, not just that it worked.

rubric.name: Iterates
rubric.description: Shows what failed first and how the next attempt changed, instead of only the final prompt.

rubric.name: Thinks like a defender
rubric.description: Can say what would have stopped the prompt: role separation, input and output guardrails, least privilege.

rubric.name: Keeps it on Gandalf
rubric.description: Treats this as a sanctioned challenge; does not carry the prompts to a real AI product or system.

outcome_logic.focus: You wrote down what worked but not why. Each level adds one guardrail, a keyword block, an output filter, a second model checking the answer; the skill is naming which one your prompt slipped past.

You kept reusing one trick. The levels are built so each technique stops working at some point; switch families, from reversal to encoding to context shifting to narrative, rather than rewording the same prompt.

You stopped at an early level. When a level blocks you, read what it refused: the refusal tells you which guardrail was added, and the deck slide for that level names the family of techniques to try next.

You used a prompt from someone else or from the internet without working out why it worked. Copying gets the password; understanding the guardrail is what you will need as the one building the defences.

You did not think about what would have stopped your prompt. For each level you beat, name the fix: keep system and user roles apart, filter the output as well as the input, give the model nothing it should not reveal.
Keep these prompts on Gandalf. It is a sanctioned training target; trying the same techniques on a real product or a company’s assistant is a different thing with different rules.
The next practice moves the injection out of the chat box and into the files an AI reads: hidden text in a CV and a photo. Same weakness, no typing required.
